title: Engine sputters or misfires
h1: Why is my engine sputtering or misfiring while driving?
metaDesc: Engine sputtering or misfiring? Answer a few questions to see if it's spark plugs, a coil, fuel or something serious, and when to stop driving.
intro: A misfire happens when one or more cylinders fail to burn their fuel properly, which you feel as a sputter, shake or stumble. Some misfires are a quick spark plug fix; others can damage the engine or exhaust if you keep driving. The questions below sort out which you're dealing with.
safety: If the check engine light is flashing, pull over when it's safe and stop driving. A severe misfire can overheat the catalytic converter.
If you smell raw fuel or see smoke, pull over, turn the engine off and step away from the car.
If the temperature gauge is in the red or there's steam from under the hood, pull over and turn the engine off.
If the engine cuts out completely while you're moving, steer to a safe spot. Steering and braking will feel heavier.

q_signs.q: Do you notice any of these along with the sputtering?
q_signs.help: The check engine light is the orange engine-shaped light on the dash. Flashing means a misfire is happening right now and is serious.

opts.a: The check engine light is flashing, or the engine shakes violently
A strong smell of raw fuel
The temperature gauge is high, or there's white smoke with a sweet smell
The check engine light is on, but steady (not flashing)

q_pattern.q: When does it sputter or misfire?

opts.a: All the time, even at idle: a steady shake or putt-putt rhythm
Mainly when accelerating, climbing a hill or carrying a load
Mostly in rain or damp weather, or on cold starts
It comes and goes, and sometimes it nearly stalls
Mostly when the fuel tank is low

q_load.help: These clues separate an ignition problem from a fuel problem.

opts.a: The spark plugs are old or I don't know when they were last changed
It started right after I filled up with fuel
It feels weak and starved, worse at highway speed or uphill
None of these / I'm not sure

result.title: A severe misfire may be happening. Stop driving to avoid damage
result.now: Pull over when it's safe and turn the engine off. Have the car towed or call a mobile mechanic.
if: If you can't stop right away, ease off the gas, avoid hard acceleration and get off the road as soon as it's safe.
If you see smoke, smell burning, or notice a glow under the car, get everyone out and away from the vehicle.
If the temperature gauge is high or the oil pressure light is on, don't restart the engine.
result.why: A flashing check engine light means misfires are severe enough to send unburned fuel into the exhaust. That fuel burns inside the catalytic converter and can overheat it, destroying it and creating a fire risk. Violent shaking usually means at least one cylinder has stopped working.

causes.name: Failed ignition coil or spark plug
causes.clues: Sudden onset, and the engine feels like it's running on fewer cylinders.

causes.name: Fuel injector stuck open or not firing
causes.clues: A fuel smell from the exhaust, or a misfire on one cylinder that doesn't move when coils are swapped.

causes.name: Mechanical damage, like a burnt valve or low compression
causes.clues: A ticking or tapping noise, or the misfire started after overheating.

shop: Code scan and misfire counts by cylinder

result.title: A fuel leak or a stuck injector is possible. Don't drive it
result.now: Pull over, turn the engine off and step away from the car. Have it towed.
if: If you see fuel dripping or pooling, move well away and call for help. Don't let anyone smoke nearby.
If the smell was brief and only right after refueling, a loose fuel cap is possible. But with the engine sputtering too, still have it checked before driving.
result.why: Sputtering together with a strong fuel smell can mean fuel is leaking onto the engine, or an injector is dumping too much fuel into a cylinder. Either way, raw fuel near hot engine and exhaust parts is a fire risk.

causes.name: Leaking fuel line, rail or injector seal
causes.clues: Wet spots on top of the engine or under the car.

causes.name: Fuel injector stuck open
causes.clues: The smell comes from the exhaust, and the engine runs very rough.

causes.name: Misfire sending unburned fuel into the exhaust
causes.clues: A flashing or steady check engine light.

you: From a safe distance, look for wet spots under the car.

result.title: Coolant may be getting into the engine, often from a head gasket problem
result.now: Pull over and turn the engine off. Don't open the radiator cap while it's hot. Have the car towed.
if: If the coolant level is low once the engine is fully cold, that supports a coolant leak. Still don't drive it until it's checked.
If you see steam or smoke from under the hood, step away from the car.
result.why: A misfire with overheating or sweet-smelling white smoke points to coolant leaking into a cylinder. Coolant doesn't burn, so that cylinder misfires. Driving an overheating engine can warp or crack major parts quickly.

causes.name: Blown head gasket
causes.clues: White smoke that smells sweet, coolant level dropping, overheating.

causes.name: Cracked cylinder head
causes.clues: The engine overheated badly before the misfire started.
causes.against: Less common than a head gasket.

causes.name: Overheating from a cooling system failure, causing misfires
causes.clues: A coolant leak, a broken belt, or a fan that isn't running.

you: Once the engine is fully cold, check the coolant level in the overflow tank.

result.title: One cylinder may not be firing, often from a coil or plug problem
result.now: If the check engine light starts flashing or the engine shakes hard, pull over when it's safe and stop driving. Otherwise: Have it checked within the next few days. Keep trips short and gentle until then.
if: If the check engine light starts flashing or the shaking gets much worse, pull over and stop driving.
If there's a ticking or tapping noise with the misfire, mention it. It may point to a valve or mechanical problem.
If you smell raw fuel or burning, see smoke, or the temperature gauge rises, pull over and turn the engine off.
If the engine nearly stalls or cuts out, stop driving it and have it checked.
result.why: A steady miss you can feel even at idle usually means one cylinder isn't firing at all. Common reasons are a failed ignition coil or spark plug, and a shop will usually read the code and swap the coil between cylinders to confirm before replacing parts. Driving on it for long wastes fuel and can damage the catalytic converter.

causes.name: Failed ignition coil
causes.clues: Sudden onset, a steady check engine light, and a code that names one cylinder.

causes.name: Worn or fouled spark plug
causes.clues: Plugs that are overdue, or oil found in the spark plug well.

causes.name: Clogged or failed fuel injector
causes.clues: The misfire stays on the same cylinder after the coil is swapped.

causes.name: Low compression in one cylinder
causes.clues: A ticking noise, or the misfire continues after coils and plugs are replaced.
causes.against: Less common than coil or plug problems.

you: Have the check engine code read. Many parts stores do this free.
shop: Code scan and misfire counts by cylinder
Injector and compression tests if needed

result.title: Possibly worn spark plugs or a weakening ignition coil
result.now: If the check engine light starts flashing or the engine shakes hard, pull over when it's safe and stop driving. Otherwise: Have the ignition system checked within the next few days, and avoid hard acceleration until then.
if: If the plugs are overdue, new plugs are a common fix, but have the codes read and the coils checked too so the right part gets replaced.
If the check engine light starts flashing, pull over and stop driving.
If you smell raw fuel or the engine nearly stalls, stop driving it and have it checked.
result.why: Under load, the engine needs a stronger spark to light the fuel. Worn plugs or a tired coil can get by at idle but miss when you accelerate, which feels like sputtering or jerking. Misfires that are left alone tend to get worse.

causes.name: Worn spark plugs
causes.clues: The plugs haven't been changed in a long time.

causes.name: Weak ignition coil or cracked coil boot
causes.clues: The misfire is worse under load, and the code names one cylinder.

causes.name: Worn spark plug wires (older cars)
causes.clues: Visible cracks on the wires, or sparking you can see in the dark.
causes.against: Many newer cars have no plug wires.

you: Check your maintenance records for the last spark plug change.
Have the check engine code read if the light is on.

result.title: Damp or cold-start misfires often point to worn ignition parts
result.now: If the check engine light starts flashing or the engine shakes hard, pull over when it's safe and stop driving. Otherwise: Book an ignition system check when convenient. Try to bring it in on a damp day or for a cold start so the shop can see it happen.
if: If the check engine light starts flashing or the engine shakes hard, pull over and stop driving.
If it only happens on the first cold start and clears in a minute, mention whether the car is driven mostly on short trips.
result.why: Moisture lets spark escape through cracked coil boots, plug wires or dirty plugs before it reaches the cylinder. Cold engines are also harder to fire, so weak ignition parts show up first in damp or cold conditions.

causes.name: Cracked coil boots or spark plug wires
causes.clues: Worse on rainy or foggy days, or after washing the engine.

causes.name: Worn or fouled spark plugs
causes.clues: Plugs that are overdue, or a car used mostly for short trips.

causes.name: Water collecting around the spark plugs
causes.clues: A clogged drain at the base of the windshield, or water pooling on top of the engine.

you: Note the weather and engine temperature each time it happens.
shop: Coil boot and plug wire inspection

result.title: The engine may not be getting enough fuel
result.now: Have it checked within the next few days. Avoid long trips and highways until then.
if: If it stalls while driving, stop driving it and have it towed. Losing power in traffic is dangerous.
If the check engine light comes on, have the code read. A lean code points toward fuel or air problems.
If you smell raw fuel, pull over, turn the engine off and step away from the car.
result.why: Sputtering that comes and goes, or that's worse when you need more power, can mean fuel supply is falling short. A weak pump or clogged filter may keep up at light throttle and then run short when demand rises. Left alone, it can leave you stranded. A shop will usually test fuel pressure and volume before replacing the pump.

causes.name: Weak or failing fuel pump
causes.clues: Worse at highway speed, uphill, or with a low tank. A whine from the rear of the car.

causes.name: Clogged fuel filter
causes.clues: Higher mileage and no record of a filter change.

causes.name: Dirty mass airflow sensor or vacuum leak
causes.clues: A rough idle, hissing under the hood, or a lean code.

you: Note whether it's worse with a low tank.
Listen for a whine from the back of the car.
shop: Code scan and fuel trim data

result.title: The engine may be running short of fuel when the tank is low
result.now: Keep the tank at least a quarter full and see if the sputtering stops.
if: If it still sputters with a fuller tank, the fuel pump or filter may need checking. Book a check within a few days.
If it stalls while driving, stop driving it and have it checked before using it again.
If you smell raw fuel, turn the engine off and have it checked before driving.
result.why: On turns, hills or hard braking, fuel sloshes away from the pump's pickup when the tank is low, and the engine briefly runs short. A pump that's getting weak shows this sooner. Keeping more fuel in the tank also helps the pump stay cool.

causes.name: Fuel sloshing away from the pickup
causes.clues: Only happens below a quarter tank, especially on curves or hills.

causes.name: Weakening fuel pump
causes.clues: A whine from the rear, or sputtering at highway speed too.

causes.name: Fuel gauge reading higher than the actual level
causes.clues: You've run out before when the gauge showed fuel left.

you: Keep the tank above a quarter for a week and note if the problem goes away.

result.title: You may have a tank of poor-quality fuel or the wrong grade
result.now: If the check engine light starts flashing or the engine shakes hard, pull over when it's safe and stop driving. Otherwise: Check your receipt for the right fuel grade, drive gently, and refill with fresh fuel from a busy station once the tank is low.
if: If you put diesel in a gas car (or gas in a diesel), stop driving it right away and have it towed. The tank will need to be drained.
If the sputtering doesn't improve after fresh fuel, have it checked. If the check engine light starts flashing, pull over and stop driving.
If you smell raw fuel or the engine shakes hard, pull over and stop driving.
result.why: Water or dirt in the fuel, makes the engine run rough and sputter. When the problem starts right after filling up, the fuel is a likely link.

causes.name: Water or contamination in the fuel
causes.clues: It started right after filling up.

causes.name: Lower octane than your engine requires
causes.clues: Your manual says premium is required and you used regular. You may hear pinging.

you: Check the fuel grade on your receipt against your owner's manual.

result.title: Get the codes read, then have the misfire diagnosed
result.now: If the check engine light starts flashing or the engine shakes hard, pull over when it's safe and stop driving. Otherwise: Have the check engine codes read (many parts stores do this free), then book a check soon and describe when the sputtering happens.
if: If the check engine light starts flashing or the engine shakes hard, pull over and stop driving.
If it sputters at idle all the time or nearly stalls, get it checked within a few days.
If you smell raw fuel, see smoke or the temperature gauge rises, pull over and turn the engine off.
result.why: Misfires come from spark, fuel or compression problems. Stored codes often name the cylinder involved, which narrows it down quickly. A note of when it happens helps the shop find the cause without guessing.

causes.name: Ignition problem (plugs, coils, wires)
causes.clues: A common cause of misfires.

causes.name: Fuel delivery problem
causes.clues: Sputtering under load or with a low tank.

causes.name: Vacuum leak or sensor problem
causes.clues: A rough idle or hissing sound.

you: Keep a note of when it happens: cold or warm, idle or accelerating, weather, fuel level.

q_fuel_type.q: Could the wrong type of fuel have gone in?
q_fuel_type.help: Check your receipt or the pump you used.

opts.a: Yes: diesel in a gas car, or gas in a diesel
No, the right type, but maybe poor quality or the wrong grade

result.title: The wrong type of fuel went in
result.now: Don’t start the engine. If it’s running, pull over when it’s safe and turn it off. Don’t restart it. Have it towed: the tank will need to be drained.
if: If you smell raw fuel, keep sparks and flames away and move away from the car.
If you realize at the pump before starting the engine, leave it off and ask the station for help moving the car.
result.why: Diesel in a gas engine, or gas in a diesel, doesn't burn the way the engine is built for. Running it can damage the fuel system and engine, so the tank and fuel lines need to be drained before it's started again.

causes.name: Diesel in a gas car
causes.clues: Heavy smoke, very rough running or the engine dying soon after filling up.

causes.name: Gas in a diesel
causes.clues: Knocking, loss of power or the engine stopping soon after filling up.

you: Check your receipt and the pump you used to confirm which fuel went in.
shop: Drain and flush the tank and fuel lines
